_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Common dry-cleaning chemical linked to triple the risk of liver scarring
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A chemical commonly used in dry cleaning and found in some household products may be an overlooked threat to liver health. Researchers found that people with detectable levels of tetrachloroethylene (PCE) in their blood were three times more likely to have significant liver fibrosis, a dangerous buildup of scar tissue that can eventually lead to liver failure or cancer. The risk climbed sharply as PCE levels increased, even after accounting for factors such as age, sex, race, education, alcohol use, and metabolic conditions.

items.title: [Fast Company] Nearly 200 Amazon workers called this pregnancy rights hotline in 2026. Now there’s a lawsuit
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Amazon is once again under fire for its work policies, this time with a new class action lawsuit filed against the retail giant on Tuesday that alleges the company has failed to make basic workplace accommodations for its pregnant employees.

The lawsuit, filed in a Brooklyn federal court, alleges that the Seattle-based company has engaged in a systematic and company-wide failure to accommodate pregnant workers and deliberately retaliated against them. The four named plaintiffs, all of whom were formerly employed at Amazon warehouses in New York, detail instances in which they claim they were denied work accommodations and subsequently disciplined or terminated, or faced retaliation during their pregnancies. 

The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, which was signed into law by President Joe Biden in 2022 and went into effect in 2023, is key to this proposed nationwide class action lawsuit. That legislation requires employers to provide “reasonable accommodations” for qualified employees affected by pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions.

The new lawsuit alleges that Amazon’s policies violated the law in two ways—by requiring a pregnant worker to provide a doctor’s note before the company will provide even basic accommodations and by failing to account for legally protected pregnancy-related breaks. The plaintiffs are represented by Emery Celli Brinckerhoff Abady Ward & Maazel LLP, a civil rights law firm, and A Better Balance, a nonprofit advocacy organization, both of which have previously been involved in legislation against the retail giant.

“As our lawsuit details, Amazon regularly violates the law. Under its policies, pregnant workers are not protected, and they face retaliation for exercising their rights,” Debbie Greenberger, a partner at Emery Celli Brinckerhoff Abady Ward & Maazel LLP, said in a statement. “Too often, pregnant women working at Amazon warehouses have to risk their health or their pregnancy just to do their jobs.”   

An Amazon spokesperson told Fast Company the company conducted “thorough” internal reviews of each of the cases referenced in the lawsuit and noted that some of the details laid out in the suit contain inaccuracies and omit important details, but didn’t provide specifics. The company also noted that in the past year, 99.9% of pregnancy accommodation requests have been approved.

“Ensuring the health and well-being of our employees is one of our greatest responsibilities, and we strive to provide a safe and supportive environment for everyone, which includes supporting tens of thousands of employees with pregnancy accommodations each year,” Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson, said in a statement to Fast Company.

AMAZON’S POLICIES UNDER SCRUTINY

Amazon states on its website that it has a mission to be “Earth’s most customer-centric company, best employer, and safest place to work.” But a long list of lawsuits and other complaints over the years have contested the latter two points, in particular. 

There are currently dozens of open cases against the company with the National Labor Relations Board and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) for a broad range of alleged violations against workers. And the new lawsuit is hardly the first time that its treatment of pregnant workers has come under scrutiny.

In October 2025, New Jersey filed a civil rights lawsuit against Amazon, alleging it systematically violated state civil rights and pregnancy protection laws across its fulfillment centers, while New York made a similar complaint in 2022 that the company was engaging in discrimination against pregnant workers by denying them reasonable accommodations.

Earlier this year, the EEOC determined that Amazon had violated both the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act and the Americans With Disabilities Act. In February, the commission determined that the company had discriminated against Jennifer Hatch, one of the plaintiffs in the class action lawsuit, by failing to provide her with pregnancy-related accommodations. 

That same determination noted there was “reasonable cause” to believe the company had likewise discriminated against “a nationwide class of female warehouse associates” since 2023. The three other plaintiffs in the lawsuit similarly filed complaints against Amazon with the EEOC.

A BIGGER THREAT

As the new lawsuit notes, the four plaintiffs are likely indicative of a bigger problem with how Amazon treats its pregnant workforce. The suit seeks reforms of Amazon’s policies on behalf of the plaintiffs and a class of “similarly situated workers,” as well as compensation for past and ongoing violations of the law. 

The number of affected workers will likely go up as word spreads about the possible class action lawsuit, and the filing notes that A Better Place fielded calls from “dozens” of pregnant Amazon employees in 2025 who said the company had denied them basic accommodations. So far this year, nearly 200 Amazon workers have called the organization’s free helpline, its president Inimai Chettiar told USA Today. 

While Amazon may be the focus of this lawsuit, it is not an isolated incident and speaks to what’s at stake if critical protections for pregnant workers are rolled back, according to Chettiar.

“It actually sits inside a larger pattern of policy and rhetoric aimed at narrowing women’s roles and pushing them out of the workforce and back into a domestic role,” she told USA Today.

items.title: [Fast Company] I was co-CEO of a $100 million company. Here’s how my sense of urgency nearly killed it
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Over the course of a long career, I’ve made my share of mistakes, but the dumbest and most damaging ones have always been driven by urgency. Whenever I convinced myself that an opportunity was so great I had to “strike while the iron is hot,” boneheaded decisions inevitably followed, usually ending in some crushing failure.

Of course, nobody ever tells you that because “creating a sense of urgency” is supposed to be a good thing. It leads to action, and action feels good. Deliberation, on the other hand, can feel frustrating and, let’s face it, boring. If you can create urgency, you can make things happen. The problem is that the things you make happen are often the wrong ones.

That was certainly true of the worst mistake I ever took part in. In 2007, our company in Kyiv hatched a plan to dominate Ukrainian-language media. At the time, there were no significant competitors, despite credible research suggesting substantial unmet demand. What looked like a once-in-a-generation opportunity turned into a catastrophe. It nearly killed the company.


The emergence of an idea

Our company, KP Media, was founded in 1995 by Jed Sunden, a 25-year-old native of Brooklyn. It started with the Kyiv Post, which he financed with $8,000 on his credit card. Mirroring the Ukrainian economy at the time, the company grew in fits for the first five or six years, but by the time I joined in 2004 it had become a significant enterprise with roughly 200 employees.  

By that time, change was in the air and our Russian-language newsweekly, Korrespondent, became very much a symbol of that change. The Orange Revolution brought not only record foreign investment to Ukraine, but also newfound interest in a free press. Ukrainian citizens—as well as advertisers—demanded accurate, objective news sources.

We dominated that market in print and online. Our business began to grow by leaps and bounds. As Ukraine became a hot market, there was increasing interest in us from investors; in 2007, we went public at a valuation of roughly $50 million, which was an enormous amount of money in Ukraine at the time. Before you knew it, our stock price doubled and we became a $100 million company.

That’s what led us to what we thought was a truly revolutionary idea. 

Ukraine had long been a bilingual country. During the Soviet era, Russian had been the official language, even though at home and with friends, most people spoke Ukrainian. But after Ukraine became an independent country in 1991, Ukrainian became the official language. On TV, programming was required to be in the Ukrainian language, but Russian-language media still dominated in print and online.

To us, the opportunity seemed obvious. If we moved early into Ukrainian-language media, just as we had in online news, we could dominate the market.

Devising a strategy

Not wanting to rely just on a hunch, we began to research the market. Historically, the most lucrative areas were in the industrial eastern provinces that were closer to Russia culturally and linguistically. But the western, more European-oriented cities, where the Ukrainian language was more deeply ingrained, were beginning to prosper. We also saw decent traffic on the Ukrainian versions of our websites. 

As we delved more deeply into the research, we found that a significant portion of the population actually preferred Ukrainian-language media. It seemed that we had identified an attractive market with pent-up demand. Because we were using publicly available research, we also expected that others would soon be rushing in to take advantage of the opportunity. There were plenty of signs that we were on to something.

So we decided to move forward aggressively. We hired an editorial director from Poland to oversee development of two women’s magazines—a monthly and a weekly. Similar in format and theme to Good Housekeeping, these were designed to appeal to women working to balance marriage, family, and work life. We also began working on a Ukrainian newsweekly to complement our hit product, Korrespondent. 

That would mean three major product launches within a year, in addition to the daily newspaper we had already launched recently. If successful, we would essentially double the size of our print media business. We knew that would stretch our resources to the limit, or even past that. Still, it seemed like a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity and we didn’t want to miss it. 

Taking the plunge

We started with the monthly women’s magazine. We hired a great team, designed the format, and developed the brand. Our sales operation pushed aggressively to secure advance commitments from advertisers and distributors. Unfortunately, both copy sales and ad sales were disappointing. Many were skeptical about the market for Ukrainian-language print media. 

Still, we had seen slow launches turn into successful products before, so we weren’t overly worried. After all, we’d done our homework, were confident in our track record of bringing original new products to market, and, as a major media company, had the marketing muscle to maintain massive promotional activity indefinitely. 

So we pressed on with the other two launches, still nervous that someone else would see the genius of our plan and copy it. Over the next six months we built out two additional editorial teams, one for the women’s weekly magazine and one for the newsweekly magazine. We built strong marketing programs for each and brought them to market. 

By summer 2008, our confidence began to wane. All three product launches had been flops. We’d also begun to hear strange murmurs about problems with the housing market in the U.S. It all seemed fairly remote to us in Ukraine, but I had some knowledgeable contacts who were beginning to speak in hushed tones about the health of the financial markets. 

We expected if there were a major global recession that Ukraine would take a hit, but its economy had been expanding by about 8% per year. We were fairly certain that even if there were a slowdown, growth would continue.

We were wrong. 

Hard lessons

Clearly, investing in Ukrainian-language magazines in 2007 was a bad decision. Launching three titles within 12 months in an unproven market was catastrophic. It very nearly killed our company. When the global financial crisis hit in 2008, the bottom fell out of the Ukrainian economy. GDP contracted a whopping 15%. The ad market dropped 85%. 

It felt apocalyptic. Every day on the way to work, I would look at the exchange kiosks showing the Ukrainian currency crashing in value. When I arrived at the office, there would be a series of excruciating decisions to make. We closed all the new brands we launched since our initial public offering. At one point, I had to fire 150 people in a day, not because they had failed us, but because we, blinded by hubris and stupidity, had failed them.

The real tragedy was that if we had been more methodical, the cash from our IPO would likely have sustained us through the crisis. In fact, having cash when very few others did would have put us in a great position. But we were sure we were on to the next big thing. We felt a profound sense of urgency to beat everyone else to the punch and moved forward at breakneck speed. 

I wish I could say I learned my lesson then, but I didn’t. The same pattern persisted. I would get excited by an idea, convince myself I was on to something important, and rush to move forward. What I learned over time is that we are incredibly poor judges of our own ideas and that we need to take a Bayesian approach, moving forward steadily, iterating and testing as we go.

The truth is that every idea is wrong. Some are off by a little, and some are off by a lot, but they are all, to some degree, wrong. The key isn’t to come up with the “right” ideas, but to make them less wrong over time.

items.title: [Fast Company] Your leaders are not okay
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A regular pattern that I have observed with my senior-level executive coaching clients is that they seem to be doing great but in reality are struggling. On the surface, they look successful: excellent results, composure under pressure, and abundant confidence in all the right settings. They wear the mask of executive presence. But underneath, they’re exhausted, and no one close to them notices or feels able to speak up.

This was brought home to me in a comment on one of my recent LinkedIn posts about the importance of human connection at work: “The person who just won Leader of the Year can be silently falling apart, and nobody notices because the performance is so good it looks like thriving. By the time it shows up on a dashboard, it’s not just expensive. It’s already downstream. Their team is carrying it. The culture is shaped by it. And nobody can name why.”

Loneliness and disconnection at work are endemic at all levels. At senior levels, these are among the most expensive, least visible problems in organizations today.

Being alone is about structure. Being lonely is about relationships

The reality of the organizational structure chart is as you move through your career, you have fewer peers, increased scrutiny, and decisions you can’t share with the broader organization. It comes with the territory. The higher you go, the fewer people can see or understand your daily reality. 

Loneliness at the top is something else entirely. It’s what happens when the structural reality of being the only person in the seat is amplified by having no one around you who sees past your title to the person underneath. There’s no one who thinks to ask how you really are, no one you can share your up and down moments with, and fewer people who listen with empathy or provide honest feedback. You’re seen as a leader first and a human second.

Being alone can be managed. But you can’t solve loneliness by changing the org chart or joining another board. Only better workplace relationships can help close the connection gap. 

Data every organization should pay attention to

The 2025 Fearless Report, based on Amy Edmondson’s research with more than 5,500 professionals in 33 countries, found that loneliness at work reduces psychological safety by half. Those who always felt lonely scored 42 on the psychological safety index, while those who never felt lonely scored 80, a 38-point difference.

When loneliness takes hold, people stop speaking up and challenging ideas. They stop having honest disagreements that raise the bar. The warning signs that something is wrong don’t disappear; people just stop voicing them. By the time the impact shows up in the numbers, the damage has been building for months.

One in 25 professionals responding to the 2025 Fearless Report shared that they always feel lonely at work. Research I conducted confirms this: In a dataset from more than 1,500 leaders, one in five reported having no meaningful workplace relationships at all. This is a leadership crisis hiding in plain sight. 

When the mask becomes the trap 

At a gathering of executive coaches, Alan Mulally, former CEO of Ford and Boeing, told a story that stuck with me. He realized that as CEO, “his face was no longer his own.” If he looked worried, people would talk: “Did you see the CEO’s face in that meeting?” Soon, it would turn into “something’s wrong.” A simple moment of concentration could become an organizational crisis by the time it reached the second floor.

As a result, leaders learn to manage their emotions, to mask what they’re really thinking and feeling. To some extent, that’s responsible leadership. As my colleague, Ruby Vesely, will often share with the leaders and teams she coaches, “Your energy affects everyone in the room and shapes what happens there. You bring the weather; are you bringing sunshine or storm clouds?” 

Being mindful of the energy you bring isn’t just for show. It’s part of your job.

But the mask that protects the organization can also trap the person wearing it. “I’m fine,” or “It’s fine,” work when things genuinely are fine. But what happens when things aren’t going according to plan? What happens when the leader behind the mask is struggling, and the mask has become so convincing that nobody thinks to look behind it? Or the leader dare not take the mask off?

I will never forget my first meeting with a CEO who was considering working with me as his coach. Within minutes he started to cry. He kept apologizing. I simply gave him the space to move through the moment. 

He was in the early days of a family bereavement, but hadn’t felt able to share that with anyone on his team. He was the poster child for “keep calm and carry on.” His mask was firmly in place, and had been for weeks, until I sensed he was carrying something heavy and asked a question that gave him permission to take it off. 

Our conversation didn’t remove his grief, but it did give him something he hadn’t had since the loss, someone who saw him as a human being first and a CEO second. 

His experience isn’t unusual. The underlying emotions behind the mask don’t fade just because they’re hidden. They ferment. Grief impacts how you show up everyday, frustration curdles into resentment, and doubt can harden into paralysis. The pressure continues to build, amplified by loneliness and the misbelief that it’s just you, that everyone else is handling this, that you’re the one who’s broken.

You’re not broken. You’re isolated, and there is a difference.

Contrary to popular belief, senior leaders are human too! They experience the same trials and tribulations as the rest of us: health scares, family crises, financial stress, self-doubt, grief. The difference is that the higher you go, the less permission you have to do any of those things publicly. “Everything’s fine” becomes the default response. And because the results are still coming in, you’re hitting your targets, nobody thinks to ask how you’re doing, only to celebrate what you’re doing. 

Until, that is, everything’s not fine, you’re not fine. And by then, the damage is already further downstream in the organization. Your team has sensed things are different, even if they can’t name what. They’ve been absorbing the stress, compensating for decisions that didn’t get made clearly, navigating conversations that never happened. The team’s culture has been shaped by a leader running on empty, and nobody can name why, because from the outside it still looked like it was thriving.

What you can do about it

This isn’t a wellness problem. And it won’t be solved by telling leaders—or yourself—to be more resilient. Resilience assumes the individual is the problem. Loneliness at the top isn’t a personal deficiency to be toughened through. It’s a relationship gap. And it requires deliberate action, intention, and attention to your relationships.

1. Start by asking yourself: Who in your professional life would tell you you’re not okay, even if you said you were? In my book, Cultivate: The Power of Winning Relationships, I call this person an Ally, a truth-speaker who supports your success no matter what. At the most senior levels, these relationships can be more challenging to maintain. Most people may choose to tell you what you want to hear because honesty can be risky. But that risk goes both ways. It can be career limiting for them if they speak up, and a career risk for you if they don’t. It’s your responsibility to nurture those relationships and the culture that allows for candor. If you can’t name your Ally, someone you can be honest with and who can be honest with you, you’re not just alone at the top, you risk being lonely.

2. Find your truth-speaker. It can be a peer from another company, a former colleague, a coach, or a mentor. What matters isn’t their rank or expertise, but their willingness to be honest with you, especially when it’s hard. If you don’t have this relationship, building it is the best investment you can make in your leadership. 

3. Stop pretending everything is “fine.” Next time someone asks how you’re doing, and you’re not okay, try giving a slightly more honest answer. You don’t have to share everything you’re thinking and feeling, but even saying, “I’m carrying a lot right now” or, “This quarter has been harder than it looks,” can be enough to create a moment of connection. When you’re honest, you encourage others to do the same.

The loneliest leaders are hiding in plain sight

They’re in your leadership meetings. They’re on stage at your company events. They’re delivering results that make everyone assume they’re fine. And they may be wondering if anyone would notice if they weren’t.

The question isn’t whether they are performing; of course they are. This is how they got to the top. The question is whether they feel connected to even one person beyond their job title, and whether anyone around them has the relationship, the courage, and care to ask what that performance is costing them.

If you’re a senior leader and this sounds at all familiar, you don’t need another program or leadership book. You need one person who can see past your results. And if you’re the colleague, board member, or friend to a senior leader, be the person who asks how they’re really doing, and stays for the real answer.

The loneliest leaders won’t tell you they’re lonely. That’s the whole point. Somebody has to go first.
